The Ghaznavid Dynasty. From 977 to 1186 of the common era, this was a Turkish military empire centered in Ghazni, in present-day Afghanistan, which conquered much of Central Asia and northern India, introducing Islam to the Indian subcontinent. Under the warrior-king Mahmud of Ghazni, the Ghaznavids became fearsome raiders and administrators, amassing wealth through Indian plunder and establishing a Turkic cultural foothold that would eventually lead to Muslim rule of India.

The dynasty was established by Alptigin in 977 in Ghazni. It rose to prominence under his successor Sabuktigin, who conquered Khorasan and the Hindu Kush region. But Mahmud of Ghazni, who ruled from 998 to 1030, became the dynasty's most celebrated ruler. He launched seventeen devastating raids into northern India, plundering temples and establishing Islam's military presence on the subcontinent. The Ghaznavids conquered the rich commercial cities of Samarkand and Bukhara, making Ghazni itself a wealthy intellectual and cultural center that rivaled Baghdad in influence. They patronized Persian poetry and literature. The poet Firdawsi composed the Shahnameh, the Book of Kings, under Ghaznavid patronage—creating one of Islam's greatest literary epics. The Ghaznavids operated as successors to the Abbasid caliphate and the earlier Samanid dynasty, maintaining the fiction of Abbasid authority while exercising independent imperial power. But they weakened under Seljuk pressure from the west and the rise of the Ghurid dynasty in Afghanistan. The empire finally collapsed in 1186, though Ghaznavid governors remained in India for another generation.

The Seljuk Empire was the rival Turkish power that pressured and eventually displaced them. The Abbasid Caliphate remained their nominal overlord. The later Mughal Empire in India inherited Ghaznavid institutional models. And the poet Firdawsi's Shahnameh became one of their enduring legacies.
